summary.text: At \(n=140\), adjacent-square bounds determine the needed floor terms and give \(a(140)=471\), \(a(144)=484\), \(a(157)=528\), and \(a(161)=542\). The claimed relation would therefore require \(542=528+484-471=541\), a contradiction.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=2n+\left\lfloor n\sqrt{\frac54}\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor\frac n4\right\rfloor
\qquad(n\geq 1).
\]
We disprove the proposed recurrence by considering its instance at \(n=140\). The recurrence would require
\[
a(161)=a(157)+a(144)-a(140).
\]
We will evaluate all four terms exactly.

We first record how the irrational floor values will be established. For positive integers \(n\) and nonnegative integers \(k\), if
\[
4k^2\leq 5n^2<4(k+1)^2,
\]
then, after division by \(4\),
\[
k^2\leq n^2\frac54<(k+1)^2.
\]
All quantities involved are nonnegative, so taking square roots preserves these inequalities, with strictness preserved in the strict inequality. Since
\[
\sqrt{n^2\frac54}=n\sqrt{\frac54},
\]
we obtain
\[
k\leq n\sqrt{\frac54}<k+1.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\left\lfloor n\sqrt{\frac54}\right\rfloor=k.
\]
We now apply this observation separately to the four needed indices.

For \(n=140\) and \(k=156\), direct integer arithmetic gives
\[
4\cdot156^2=97344<98000=5\cdot140^2<98596=4\cdot157^2.
\]
Thus
\[
\left\lfloor140\sqrt{\frac54}\right\rfloor=156.
\]
Also \(\lfloor140/4\rfloor=35\). Hence
\[
a(140)=2\cdot140+156+35=280+156+35=471.
\]

For \(n=144\) and \(k=160\), we have
\[
4\cdot160^2=102400<103680=5\cdot144^2<103684=4\cdot161^2.
\]
Therefore
\[
\left\lfloor144\sqrt{\frac54}\right\rfloor=160.
\]
Since \(\lfloor144/4\rfloor=36\), it follows that
\[
a(144)=2\cdot144+160+36=288+160+36=484.
\]

For \(n=157\) and \(k=175\), the relevant inequalities are
\[
4\cdot175^2=122500<123245=5\cdot157^2<123904=4\cdot176^2.
\]
They imply
\[
\left\lfloor157\sqrt{\frac54}\right\rfloor=175.
\]
Moreover, \(157=4\cdot39+1\), so \(\lfloor157/4\rfloor=39\). Consequently,
\[
a(157)=2\cdot157+175+39=314+175+39=528.
\]

Finally, for \(n=161\) and \(k=180\), we have
\[
4\cdot180^2=129600<129605=5\cdot161^2<131044=4\cdot181^2.
\]
Thus
\[
\left\lfloor161\sqrt{\frac54}\right\rfloor=180.
\]
As \(161=4\cdot40+1\), we also have \(\lfloor161/4\rfloor=40\). It follows that
\[
a(161)=2\cdot161+180+40=322+180+40=542.
\]

The right-hand side demanded by the proposed recurrence at \(n=140\) is instead
\[
a(157)+a(144)-a(140)=528+484-471=1012-471=541.
\]
Therefore
\[
a(161)=542\neq541=a(157)+a(144)-a(140).
\]
Since \(140\geq1\), this is an admissible instance of the universally quantified conjecture. Hence the claim that
\(a(n+21)=a(n+17)+a(n+4)-a(n)\) for every \(n\geq1\) is false.
